children: Lean hog futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange fell to life-of-contract lows on Monday, pressured by slumping wholesale pork prices and expectations of a seasonal rise in pork production, analysts said.

CME October lean hog futures (LHV26) settled down 1.925 cents at 79.600 cents per pound after hitting a contract low at 79.175 cents, and December hogs (LHZ26) ended down 1.450 cents at 71.250 cents after notching a contract low at 70.025 cents.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture priced the pork carcass cutout at $89.78 per hundredweight, down 2 cents from Friday and the lowest reading since April 2025.

"The fourth quarter is typically a struggle for the industry," said Don Roose, president of Iowa-based U.S. Commodities, noting that the most hogs are normally available for slaughter late in the year.
"The cutout doesn't move up, and (with) fear of fourth-quarter supplies coming at us, (futures) just anchored back into contract lows," Roose said.
Inter-market spreading appeared to add pressure, Roose said, with traders buying cattle futures and selling hogs.
Meanwhile, CME live cattle futures rose to one-month highs, buoyed by improved packer margins and optimism for firm cash cattle prices this week.

finished 5.350 cents higher at 337.850 cents per pound.

Beef packers were earning about $120.80 per head of cattle, according to Denver-based livestock marketing advisory service HedgersEdge.com LLC, down from $155.55 on Friday but up from $110.75 at the end of August. Packer margins were negative over most of the spring and summer.
